    Create your first plugin

    This walkthrough builds plugins from small, complete files. Start with Lesson 1 if you only need new property coefficients. Continue to Lessons 2 and 3 when you need to write an equation.

    Lesson What you create Files you write
    1. A species using built-in equations Your own nitrogen properties One YAML file
    2. A new property equation NH3 with a custom heat-capacity/enthalpy equation A manifest and one Python module
    3. A reaction N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3 with an editable rate coefficient One more Python module and a short manifest entry

    Each lesson ends with something you can register in the application. The coefficients and rate law are illustrative, not validated property datasets or an industrial ammonia model. General usage, units, API details, and troubleshooting are in the plugin guide.

    Before you start

    For Lesson 1, you need a text editor and the desktop application. Alternatively, you can create a species entirely in the application using Create plugin / Add species.

    For Lessons 2 and 3, use the source installation (online) and activate its Python environment. Run the terminal commands below from the repository root, the folder containing pyproject.toml. The supplied factories keep DAETools imports inside symbolic methods, so generating metadata and running their numerical checks does not require loading the solver. Simulations do.

    The paths below use a workspace called build/plugin-workshop. For Lesson 1, you can use any writable folder instead; no source checkout is needed. For Lessons 2 and 3, create that workspace inside the repository so the terminal commands match. Use your file manager or editor to create the folders and files. build/ is ignored by Git, so keep a separate copy of work you want to retain or share. Save files as UTF-8 plain text with their exact extensions: manifest.yaml, not manifest.yaml.txt.

    Lesson 1: create a plugin with one file

    1. Create the folder and manifest

    Inside build/plugin-workshop, create a folder called my_nitrogen. Create my_nitrogen/manifest.yaml with this complete content:

    id: my_nitrogen
name: My nitrogen properties
source: Tutorial example; illustrative Cp coefficients.
species:
  N2:
    name: Nitrogen
    chemical_key: N2
    phase: gas
    mw: 0.0280134
    temperature_range: [298.15, 1200.0]
    enthalpy:
      model: builtin:polynomial
      parameters:
        coefficients: [30.0, 0.004, 0.000001]
        t_ref: 298.15
        h_form_ref: 0.0
    viscosity:
      model: builtin:quadratic_viscosity
      parameters:
        t_ref: 1000.0
        a0: 4.15082118e-5
        a1: 2.78501267e-8
        a2: -6.09391431e-12

    That is the entire plugin. The molecular weight and viscosity are taken from the built-in nitrogen definition; the heat-capacity coefficients are illustrative.

    The fields you are most likely to change are:

    Field Purpose
    id: my_nitrogen Identifies this plugin. Use a new ID for a separate plugin, and keep it for later updates.
    name The label shown in the plugin browser.
    species: N2: The species' local ID; its full reference is my_nitrogen:N2.
    chemical_key: N2 Identifies this as nitrogen, so it can fill an N2 reaction role or replace built-in nitrogen.
    mw Molecular weight in kg/mol.
    enthalpy.parameters This species' property coefficients, reference temperature, and reference enthalpy.
    source Where the values came from; replace the tutorial note with your scientific source for real data.

    Here Cp = 30 + 0.004 (T − 298.15) + 0.000001 (T − 298.15)², in J/(mol·K). The application integrates Cp to obtain molar enthalpy, with h(298.15 K) = 0. The declared temperature interval is in K. Gas species also need viscosity; solid species omit the viscosity entry.

    2. Register it and use it

    1. Open a project and choose Plugins → Register plugin….
    2. Select build/plugin-workshop/my_nitrogen/manifest.yaml.
    3. Confirm that My nitrogen properties appears as Enabled. Expand it and select Nitrogen to inspect your definition.
    4. To change an existing case, select this new nitrogen and choose Use this as replacement…, choose the existing nitrogen definition, and review the affected cases. If no case uses nitrogen yet, add your nitrogen from the species picker in a case's Chemistry tab.

    Checkpoint: the case's nitrogen definition comes from My nitrogen properties. Merely registering the plugin does not select it in a case.

    3. Edit and share it

    Try changing 30.0 to 31.0 in the coefficients. Register the same manifest again and accept replacement of the project's copy. The top-level id stays my_nitrogen. You can also double-click the plugin species in the application and edit its coefficients there.

    To share the current project copy, select the plugin and choose Export…. This produces a .msplugin archive that another user can register.

    You can stop here if built-in property equations meet your needs. The supplied nitrogen oxides manifest (online) follows this same pattern, adding NO and NO2 alongside the N2 variant. Quote 'NO' in YAML: unquoted NO is read as a boolean.

    Prepare the Python authoring tools

    The remaining lessons define equations in Python. You will write their parameters and reactions once in Python and let the application library generate the manifest's browsing metadata.

    Save the following complete script as build/plugin-workshop/build_plugin.py, outside the plugin folders:

    import argparse
from pathlib import Path

from packed_bed.plugins.check import check_package, generate_metadata
from packed_bed.plugins.storage import package_hash, pack_plugin

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
    description="Generate metadata, check, and package a plugin you are authoring."
)
parser.add_argument("folder", type=Path, help="Folder containing manifest.yaml")
parser.add_argument("archive", type=Path, help="Output .msplugin path outside that folder")
args = parser.parse_args()

generate_metadata(args.folder)
# Execute this particular local package for the authoring check.
# This does not save desktop approval or grant approval to recipients.
check_package(args.folder, approved=(package_hash(args.folder),))
archive = pack_plugin(args.folder, args.archive)
print("Checks passed.")
print(f"Created {archive}")

    This is a helper you create for the tutorial, not a preinstalled command. It executes the package's Python factories, rewrites manifest.yaml with their declarations, checks the package, and creates the archive. Run it on your own authoring files. The first argument is a folder, not its manifest file.

    The same script also packages Lesson 1:

    python build/plugin-workshop/build_plugin.py build/plugin-workshop/my_nitrogen dist/plugin-workshop/my_nitrogen.msplugin

    It should print Checks passed. and the archive path. The output directory is created automatically. Keep the source folder for editing; the archive is what you distribute.

    Lesson 2: write a new property equation

    Now create NH3 with a heat capacity that approaches a high-temperature limit:

    Cp(T) = cp_inf − deficit (t_ref/T)²
h(T)  = h_ref + cp_inf (T − t_ref)
        + deficit t_ref² (1/T − 1/t_ref)

    The second equation is the exact integral of the first, anchored at h_ref. This is the same model used in the supplied ammonia example (online).

    1. Describe the species and point to the equation

    Create build/plugin-workshop/my_ammonia/manifest.yaml:

    id: my_ammonia
name: My ammonia model
source: Tutorial example; properties and kinetics are illustrative.
species:
  NH3:
    name: Ammonia
    chemical_key: NH3
    phase: gas
    mw: 0.01703052
    temperature_range: [298.15, 1200.0]
    enthalpy:
      model: inverse_square
      parameters:
        cp_inf: 70.0
        deficit: 35.0
        t_ref: 298.15
        h_ref: -46000.0
    viscosity:
      model: builtin:quadratic_viscosity
      parameters:
        t_ref: 298.15
        a0: 1.0e-5
        a1: 3.0e-8
        a2: 0.0
correlations:
  inverse_square:
    name: Inverse-square Cp
    kind: enthalpy
    implementation: enthalpy:create

    The connection is:

    NH3.enthalpy.model: inverse_square
    → correlations.inverse_square
    → enthalpy:create
    → create(parameters) in enthalpy.py

    enthalpy.parameters supplies values for NH3. The correlation's declarations (defaults, units, descriptions, and bounds) will be generated from Python. Finish the next two steps before registering this manifest.

    2. Write the equation

    Create build/plugin-workshop/my_ammonia/enthalpy.py with this complete content:

    from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np
from packed_bed.plugins import BaseCorrelation, ParameterSpec

PARAMETERS = {
    "cp_inf": ParameterSpec(70.0, "J/(mol*K)", "High-temperature Cp", minimum=1),
    "deficit": ParameterSpec(35.0, "J/(mol*K)", "Cp deficit at Tref", minimum=0),
    "t_ref": ParameterSpec(298.15, "K", "Reference temperature", minimum=1),
    "h_ref": ParameterSpec(-46000.0, "J/mol", "Enthalpy at Tref"),
}


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class InverseSquareEnthalpy(BaseCorrelation):
    cp_inf: float
    deficit: float
    t_ref: float
    h_ref: float

    def _cp(self, t):
        return self.cp_inf - self.deficit * (self.t_ref / t)**2

    def _h(self, t):
        return (
            self.h_ref
            + self.cp_inf * (t - self.t_ref)
            + self.deficit * self.t_ref**2 * (1 / t - 1 / self.t_ref)
        )

    def value(self, temperature):
        return self._h(np.asarray(temperature, dtype=float))

    def cp_value(self, temperature):
        return self._cp(np.asarray(temperature, dtype=float))

    def dae_expression(self, temperature):
        from daetools.pyDAE import Constant
        from pyUnits import J, K, mol
        return self._h(temperature / Constant(1 * K)) * Constant(1 * J / mol)

    def cp_dae_expression(self, temperature):
        from daetools.pyDAE import Constant
        from pyUnits import J, K, mol
        return self._cp(temperature / Constant(1 * K)) * Constant(1 * J / (mol * K))


def create(parameters):
    if parameters["deficit"] >= parameters["cp_inf"]:
        raise ValueError("Cp at Tref must be positive: deficit must be smaller than cp_inf.")
    return InverseSquareEnthalpy(**parameters)

    There are three jobs here:

    1. PARAMETERS declares the values users may edit, including their units and bounds.
    2. The class evaluates the same equations numerically and symbolically. Numerical methods use NumPy and accept arrays. The solver methods normalize temperature to K and attach the output units.
    3. create(parameters) checks the relationship between two parameters and returns the correlation object. The application supplies this dictionary.

    When adapting the example, begin with _cp, its integral _h, and the parameter declarations. Keep numerical and symbolic results consistent. More complex expressions may need separate numerical and DAETools functions; the logarithmic example (online) shows np.log and DAETools Log.

    3. Generate, check, and package it

    Run this from the repository root in your active Python environment:

    python build/plugin-workshop/build_plugin.py build/plugin-workshop/my_ammonia dist/plugin-workshop/my_ammonia.msplugin

    Checkpoint: the command prints Checks passed. and creates dist/plugin-workshop/my_ammonia.msplugin. Open the source manifest: the correlations.inverse_square.parameters declarations have been filled in. You keep editing the equation and declarations in Python; regenerate instead of manually synchronizing those generated entries.

    Register the completed manifest or archive. Select My ammonia model, choose Enable, allow your code, and wait for Checks passed. Its Ammonia species is now available in Chemistry. Double-click the species in Plugins to see the custom correlation's editable parameters.

    4. Check that the equation behaves as intended

    A package check verifies the software contract. Also check your equation. Save this as build/plugin-workshop/check_enthalpy.py, beside my_ammonia:

    import numpy as np
from my_ammonia.enthalpy import PARAMETERS, create

parameters = {key: spec.default for key, spec in PARAMETERS.items()}
correlation = create(parameters)
temperature = np.linspace(parameters["t_ref"], 1200.0, 100)
enthalpy = correlation.value(temperature)
cp = correlation.cp_value(temperature)

assert enthalpy.shape == temperature.shape
assert cp.shape == temperature.shape
assert np.all(np.isfinite(enthalpy))
assert np.all(np.isfinite(cp)) and np.all(cp > 0)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    correlation.value(parameters["t_ref"]), parameters["h_ref"]
)

step = 0.01
numerical_derivative = (
    correlation.value(temperature + step) - correlation.value(temperature - step)
) / (2 * step)
np.testing.assert_allclose(numerical_derivative, cp, rtol=1e-7)
print("Enthalpy reference, array output, positive Cp, and dh/dT checks passed.")

    Run:

    python build/plugin-workshop/check_enthalpy.py

    This checks the default parameters. Also test any different species parameter sets you supply. Before using a new correlation scientifically, compare the symbolic implementation with the numerical one and verify it against its source data. This small numerical check does not test the solver.

    Lesson 3: add a reaction

    Keep the my_ammonia folder from Lesson 2. Add a simple reaction:

    N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3
r = k c_N2 c_H2

    Concentrations are in mol/m³ bed, and r is in mol/(m³ bed·s). The model is irreversible, first order in each reactant, and has no catalyst, temperature dependence, or equilibrium term.

    1. Write the rate and reaction definition

    Create build/plugin-workshop/my_ammonia/kinetics.py:

    from packed_bed.plugins import ParameterSpec, ReactionDefinition, ReactionFamily

PARAMETERS = {
    "k": ParameterSpec(
        0.001, "m^3 bed/(mol*s)",
        "Rate coefficient using concentrations per bed volume", minimum=0,
    ),
}


def rate(context):
    from daetools.pyDAE import Constant, Max
    from pyUnits import m, mol, s

    model, cell = context.model, context.idx_cell
    zero = Constant(0 * mol / m**3)
    nitrogen = Max(model.c_gas(context.gas_index("N2"), cell), zero)
    hydrogen = Max(model.c_gas(context.gas_index("H2"), cell), zero)
    return Constant(context.parameters["k"] * m**3 / (mol * s)) * nitrogen * hydrogen


def create(parameters):
    reaction = ReactionDefinition(
        id="synthesis",
        name="N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3",
        phase="gas_gas",
        stoichiometry={"N2": -1, "H2": -3, "NH3": 2},
        required_species=("N2", "H2", "NH3"),
        source_reference="Illustrative plugin example",
        notes="Irreversible, first order in each reactant. No catalyst, equilibrium or pressure fit.",
    )
    return ReactionFamily(
        name="Ammonia synthesis",
        reactions=(reaction,),
        required_gas_species=("N2", "H2", "NH3"),
        required_solid_species=(),
        kinetics_hooks={"synthesis": rate},
    )

    You define the chemistry in ReactionDefinition and the equation in rate. ReactionFamily joins them: the "synthesis" key in kinetics_hooks must match the reaction's id.

    The factory must accept parameters; this rate reads its values later through context.parameters. The index helpers resolve roles to whichever components the case has bound to N2 and H2. Max protects against negative trial concentrations during solving.

    The engine multiplies your extent rate by stoichiometry: the species sources are −r for N2, −3r for H2, and +2r for NH3. The coefficient −3 does not make the rate third order in H2; a different order must be written in the rate equation.

    2. Add its factory to the manifest

    Append this at the top level of my_ammonia/manifest.yaml, aligned with species: and correlations::

    mechanisms:
  synthesis:
    name: Ammonia synthesis
    implementation: kinetics:create

    Do not copy the reaction's stoichiometry or parameter declarations into YAML. Run the same build command again:

    python build/plugin-workshop/build_plugin.py build/plugin-workshop/my_ammonia dist/plugin-workshop/my_ammonia.msplugin

    The generated manifest now includes the reaction, gas roles, and k declaration. Your complete source folder is:

    build/plugin-workshop/
├── build_plugin.py
├── check_enthalpy.py
├── my_nitrogen/
│   └── manifest.yaml
└── my_ammonia/
    ├── manifest.yaml
    ├── enthalpy.py
    └── kinetics.py

    3. Select the reaction in a case

    Register the updated manifest or archive and confirm replacement of the project's copy. Adding kinetics.py changes the code, so allow it when prompted.

    In the case's Chemistry tab:

    1. Select built-in N2 and H2, and Ammonia from My ammonia model.
    2. Choose + Add reaction families… and add Ammonia synthesis from your plugin.
    3. Select its N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3 reaction and inspect Bindings….
    4. Supply the case's gas compositions and solid-bed configuration. For example, use an inert solid bed and a feed of 0.25 N2 / 0.75 H2 / 0 NH3, within the example's 298.15–1200 K temperature interval. Complete the other reactor and operating inputs before running.

    Checkpoint: the family and reaction appear in Chemistry, with NH3 bound to your plugin species. This lesson defines the plugin; the feed suggestion is not a complete reactor case.

    4. Change a rate parameter without rewriting code

    In Plugins, select your synthesis reaction and choose Edit…. Change k from 0.001 to 0.002, then save. At the same concentrations the rate doubles.

    To make that change in your source files instead, add values to the existing mechanisms.synthesis entry:

        values:
      k: 0.002

    Keep the generated fields already in that entry. Run the build command and re-register. values.k overrides the default for this plugin; the default declaration remains 0.001. Changing the value needs no new code approval. Changing Python parameter names, defaults, units, bounds, or reaction declarations requires metadata regeneration and re-registration.

    To create a separate model, copy the folder and change its top-level id and name. To add another reaction to the same family, create another ReactionDefinition, add it to reactions, and add its rate function to kinetics_hooks. Include every species the rate reads in the reaction's required_species and the family's gas/solid roles.

    Use the supplied examples as templates

    The repository also contains complete, ready-to-register packages:

    Folder What it demonstrates Files to start with
    nitrogen_oxides (online) Several species using built-in equations, including an N2 variant manifest.yaml (online)
    ammonia (online) The custom property equation and rate law built in Lessons 2–3 manifest.yaml (online), enthalpy.py (online), kinetics.py (online)
    enthalpy_overrides (online) Two species sharing a custom correlation with different parameter values manifest.yaml (online), correlation.py (online)

    Each folder is independent. You may register its manifest directly; the Python examples need Enable and local code approval. Registering them does not automatically replace any case definitions.

    For the CO2/H2O example:

    1. Copy enthalpy_overrides into your workspace and give its manifest a new id and name if you want an independent plugin.
    2. Read correlation.py. It uses Cp = cp_inf − deficit t_ref/T and h = h_ref + cp_inf (T − t_ref) − deficit t_ref log(T/t_ref).
    3. Edit the CO2 or H2O enthalpy.parameters in the manifest. Each species has its own coefficients despite using the same logarithmic correlation.
    4. Build with the helper script, register, and enable it. Select the plugin's Carbon Dioxide or Water, then Use this as replacement… to apply it to existing compatible case definitions.

    Those species retain the built-in molecular weights, viscosities, and reference enthalpies; the Cp curves are illustrative replacements. Their shared code does not require installing a separate correlation plugin.

    Share your finished example

    If you edited source files, share the archive created by build_plugin.py. If you edited the project copy in the application, use Export… from Plugins to share those edits. These are separate copies, so choose the one you changed.

    Include a README describing the equations, units, source data, intended range, and known limitations. Recipients register the archive and approve Python code locally. For changes to an existing plugin, keep its id; for a separate alternative, give it a new one.
